CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Soil is the upper layer of the earth where plants grow.
It is one of the essential components of land.
It consists of particles of rock, different kinds of soil and organic material.
CHARACTERISTICS OF SANDY SOIL
1. It has large, loosely packed particles.
2. It does not hold water.
3. It is rough when rubbed between fingers.
4. Crops do not grow well on sandy soil.
5. Sandy soils are light brown.
LESSON 2 - CHARACTERISTICS OF CLAY SOIL
1. It has small and closely packed particles.
2. It is smooth when dry and sticky when wet.
3. It can hold a lot of nutrients.
4. It does not allow air and water through it.
5. It can hold water.
6. Most crops do not grow well on it.
CHARACTERISTICS OF LOAMY SOIL
1. It is very fertile.
2. It contains different minerals and nutrients.
3. It has good drainage capability.
4. It is consistency.

LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Soil is the upper layer of the earth where plants grow.
It is one of the essential components of land. There different soil types - sandy, clay and loamy soils.
It consists of particles of rock, different kinds of soil and organic material. Each of the soil type contains mineral particles, organic matter, water and air which determine physical properties of soil.
PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF SOIL
The physical properties of soil are -
- Texture
- Structure
- Porosity
- Chemistry
- Colour
LESSON 2 - PROPERTIES OF SOIL
1. TEXTURE
Soil texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay sized particles. In this case, sand particles are the largest and clay particles the smallest.
2. STRUCTURE
Soil structure is the arrangement of soil particles such as sand, silt, clay and organic matter into larger aggregate of various sizes and shape.
3. POROSITY
Soil porosity is the soil pore space are the small voids between soil particles that allow water to pass through.
The void between soil retain water, oxygen, and nutrients needed for plants growth.
4. CHEMISTRY
Soil chemistry is the soil science that deals with mineral composition, organic matter and environmental factors.
This will determine what will grow and how well it will grow.
5. COLOUR
Soil color is affected by the minerals present and by the organic matter content. Soil colour range from grey, black, brown, red, etc.
It does not affect the plant growth, behavior and the use of soil.

LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Soil is the upper layer of the earth where plants grow. There different soil types. The most fertility soil is loamy soil. While other soils are used for other purposes.
MEANING OF SOIL FERTILITY
Soil fertility is the ability of soil to sustain agricultural plant growth by providing essential plant nutrients.
When the soil loss its fertility, it can support agricultural plants.
CAUSES OF LOSS IN SOIL FERTILITY
1. Burning
2. Leaching
3. Overgrazing
4. Land Cleaning/Clearing
5. Excessive use of chemicals
6. Deforestation
7. Erosion
ASSIGNMENT
Find out how the bush burning, leaching, overgrazing, land clearing, etc. causes loss in soil fertility.
LESSON 2 - CAUSES OF LOSS IN SOIL FERTILITY (CONTINUITY)
1. BUSH BURNING
Bush burning is the use of fire to remove natural vegetation that protect the soil.
Bush burning destroyed the soil and organic materials of the soil. Soil never recovered easy after bush burning. It will take time or years before the soil recovered its nutrients.
2. LEACHING
Leaching is when the soil nutrients are drained because of too much of water.
3. OVERGRAZING
Overgrazing is when too many animals continuously and repeatedly eaten up the grass covered.
This culture will exposed the soil nutrients to sunlight, wind and water erosion. Finally, destroyed the soil nutrients.
4. LAND CLEARING
Land cleaning is the deliberate removal of natural vegetation by man for different purposes.
These activities expose the soil nutrients to sunlight and erosion.
5. EXCESSIVE USE OF CHEMICAL
Insecticide, pesticides and chemical fertilizer are good chemicals for controlling insects, pests and improving crop yields.
Excessive use of chemicals can affect the micro organisms in the soil.
6. DEFORESTATION
Deforestation is the cutting down of trees for economic purposes.
This practice if not controlled will expose the soil nutrients to leaching and erosion.
7. EROSION
Erosion is a washing away of top layer of the soil.
Soil erosion is inevitable after bushing burning, leaching, overgrazing and clean clearing.
The loose and unprotected soil is easily away soil and all its nutrients.

WAYS OF MAKING THE SOIL FERTILE
Soil can be make fertile in the following ways:
1. Adding fertilizer
2. Mulching
3. Crop rotation
4. leaving fallow
5. Afforestation
LESSON 2 - HOW TO MAINTAIN SOIL FERTILITY
1. ADDING FERTILIZER
Fertilizer is an organic and inorganic materials that is added to the soil to supply plant nutrients.
Organic materials are decayed death plants and animals and their waste products in the environment. While inorganic materials are chemical compound.
2. MULCHING
Mulching is a layer materials that is spread on top of the soil to protect the soil nutrients.
Mulching is very important because,
- it preserves the soil moisture
- it improves fertility and and health of the soil
- it reduces weed growth, and
- it enhances the visual appeal of the area.
3. CROP ROTATION
Crop rotation is the practice of growing different crops on a piece of land at different seasons.
The planting of a particular crop this season will not be planted next season on the same land.
4. LAND FALLOW
Fallow is the practice of leaving agricultural land for about a season or more without planting to naturally recover its nutrients.
5. AFFORESTATION
Afforestation is the planning of new trees across the land without trees.
It is also a common practice that proceed deforestation.

LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Soil fertility is the ability of soil to sustain agricultural plant growth by providing essential plant nutrients.
One of the ways of improving soil fertility is using compost or manure.
MEANING OF COMPOST AND MANURE
Compost and manure are used as a fertilizer for growing plants.
The different between compost and manure is the content.
Compost is made of decayed organic materials such as leaves, grasses, etc.
Organic materials are materials from plants.
While manure are the animals dung, feces, urine, death animals, etc.
METHODS OF MAKING COMPOST AND MANURE
1. Heap method
2. Pit method
HEAP METHOD
Heap compost is the method of making compost on open surface area.
MATERIALS NEEDED FOR MAKING COMPOST
1. Dried plants such as leaves, grasses, flowers, decayed fruits or seeds, weeds, etc.
2. Sewage
3. Farmyard waste
4. Sand dust (little)
5. Soil
6. Water
LESSON 2 - MAKING COMPOST USING HEAP METHOD
Organize the pupils into groups, guide them to adequately mix up the organic materials on open surface area far away from the classroom to avoid bad odour.
MATERIALS NEEDED FOR MAKING MANURE
Manures are the animals dung, feces, urine, death animals, etc.
They are ready to use materials unless to dry if wet.

1. Dig a dip pit

4. Add water and cover with soil.

MEANING AND IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE
AGRICULTURE

ENTRY BEHAVIOUR

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People depend on agriculture for many things they use every day. Farmers grow crops, rear animals, catch or rear fish, keep bees, and manage forests to provide useful products.
Agriculture provides food, employment, income, and raw materials for industries. It also contributes to the development of communities and the country.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning of agriculture, examples of agricultural activities, and the importance of agriculture.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF AGRICULTURE
Agriculture is the practice of cultivating crops and rearing animals for food, raw materials, income, and other useful purposes.
Agriculture involves activities such as crop production, animal production, fishing, forestry, and the processing of agricultural products.
EXAMPLES OF AGRICULTURAL ACTIVITIES
Agricultural activities include,
- Growing maize: Planting and harvesting maize.
- Planting cassava: Growing cassava for food and other uses.
- Rearing goats and cattle: Keeping goats and cattle for useful products.
- Poultry farming: Keeping birds such as chickens for eggs and meat.
- Fishing: Catching fish from rivers, lakes, seas, or ponds.
- Fish farming: Rearing fish in ponds or tanks.
- Beekeeping: Keeping bees to produce honey.
- Forestry: Planting and managing trees for useful products.
LESSON 2 - IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE
Agriculture is important because it:
1. Provides food: It provides crops, meat, fish, milk, eggs, and other food products.
2. Provides employment: Many people work as farmers, farm labourers, traders, processors, and agricultural professionals.
3. Provides raw materials: Agricultural products such as cotton, rubber, cocoa, and palm products are used as raw materials in industries.
4. Provides income: Farmers and other people involved in agriculture earn money from agricultural activities.
5. Supports industries: Industries depend on agricultural products for processing and manufacturing.
6. Promotes economic development: Agriculture contributes to the growth of the economy.
7. Provides foreign exchange: Some agricultural products are exported to other countries and generate foreign exchange.
8. Provides materials for clothing: Crops such as cotton provide materials used in making clothes.
9. Provides useful products: Agriculture provides products such as timber, leather, palm oil, and rubber.
10. Supports rural development: Agricultural activities create businesses and improve economic activities in rural communities.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Agriculture is an important part of human life because it provides food, employment, income, raw materials, and other useful products.
- It also contributes to the development of communities and the Nigerian economy.

They also learned that agriculture is important because it provides food, employment, income, and raw materials and contributes to the development of the country.

The teacher asks pupils:

In this lesson, pupils will learn about agriculture as a source of food, sources of manufactured products from agriculture, and the nutritional values of some agricultural produce.
AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF FOOD
Agriculture is an important source of food for humans. Farmers grow crops and rear animals that provide different types of food for people.
Examples include:
- Crops: Maize, rice, cassava, yam, beans, vegetables, and fruits.
- Animals: Cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, and poultry provide meat and other products.
- Fish: Fish farming and fishing provide fish for human consumption.
- Eggs and milk: Poultry and cattle provide eggs and milk.
- Honey: Bees produce honey, which is used as food.
IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF FOOD
Agriculture:
1. Provides food for people.
2. Provides different types of food for a balanced diet.
3. Helps prevent hunger and food shortages.
4. Provides fresh fruits and vegetables.
5. Provides meat, fish, eggs, and milk.
6. Provides food for families and communities.
7. Provides income for farmers to buy food and other necessities.
8. Supports food processing and preservation.
SOURCES OF MANUFACTURED PRODUCE FROM AGRICULTURE
Agricultural products are used as raw materials to manufacture many useful products.
Agricultural Produce - Manufactured Products
1. Cotton - Clothes and textiles
2. Cocoa - Chocolate and cocoa products
3. Rubber - Tyres and rubber products
4. Palm oil - Soap and cosmetics
5. Cassava - Garri, flour, and starch
6. Milk - Cheese, yoghurt, and other dairy products
7. Leather from animals - Shoes, bags, and belts
8. Timber - Furniture and paper products
NUTRITIONAL VALUES OF SOME AGRICULTURAL PRODUCE
Agricultural produce contains nutrients needed for healthy growth and development.
1. Maize: Provides carbohydrates and some vitamins and minerals. It gives the body energy.
2. Beans: Provides protein, fibre, vitamins, and minerals. It helps build and repair body tissues.
3. Eggs: Rich in protein, vitamins, and minerals. They support growth and body development.
4. Milk: Provides protein and calcium. It helps build strong bones and teeth.
5. Fish: Provides protein and healthy fats. It supports growth and body development.
6. Meat: Provides protein, iron, and other nutrients needed for growth and healthy blood.
7. Fruits: Provide vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water. They help keep the body healthy.
8. Vegetables: Provide vitamins, minerals, and fibre. They support good health and proper body functions.
9. Cassava: Mainly provides carbohydrates and energy.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Agriculture provides many of the foods people eat every day.
- It also supplies raw materials for manufacturing products such as clothes, soap, chocolate, tyres, furniture, shoes, and dairy products.
- Agricultural produce also provides important nutrients that help people grow, stay healthy, and have energy.

Pupils have previously learned about agriculture as a source of food, manufactured products, and nutrients. This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how agriculture provides employment and income to farmers and other people.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Agriculture provides food and useful raw materials, but it also provides jobs and income for many people. Farmers grow crops, rear animals, keep fish, and carry out other agricultural activities to earn a living.
People also work in areas such as food processing, transportation, marketing, and the supply of farm inputs. Farmers earn income by selling crops, animals, fish, eggs, milk, and other agricultural products.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about agriculture as a source of employment and a source of income to the farmer.
LESSON 1 - AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF EMPLOYMENT
Agriculture provides jobs and work opportunities for many people. People can work directly on farms or in businesses connected with agriculture.
Examples of agricultural employment include:
- Crop farming: Growing crops such as maize, cassava, and yam.
- Animal farming: Rearing animals such as goats, cattle, and sheep.
- Poultry farming: Rearing chickens and other birds.
- Fish farming: Rearing fish in ponds and tanks.
- Fishing: Catching fish from rivers, lakes, and other water bodies.
- Beekeeping: Keeping bees for honey production.
- Agricultural processing: Processing farm produce into useful products.
- Agricultural marketing: Buying and selling farm produce.
LESSON 2 - AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF INCOME TO THE FARMER
Agriculture provides farmers with money earned from selling farm produce and animals. Farmers can sell their products in local markets, shops, processing companies, or to other buyers.
Examples include:
- Selling maize, rice, cassava, yam, and vegetables
- Selling goats, cattle, sheep, pigs, and poultry
- Selling eggs and milk
- Selling fish
- Selling honey
- Selling processed agricultural products.
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF EMPLOYMENT
Agriculture:
1. Provides jobs for farmers.
2. Provides work for farm labourers.
3. Creates jobs in food processing.
4. Provides employment in agricultural marketing.
5. Creates opportunities for transportation of farm produce.
6. Supports businesses that supply farm inputs and equipment.
IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF INCOME
Agriculture:
1. Provides income for farmers.
2. Helps farmers meet their daily needs.
3. Enables farmers to pay school fees and medical expenses.
4. Helps farmers improve their farms.
5. Supports family welfare.
6. Provides money for starting or expanding other businesses.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Agriculture is an important source of employment and income.
- It provides jobs for farmers and other workers while allowing farmers to earn money by selling crops, animals, fish, and other agricultural products.

SUMMARY
Pupils learned that agriculture is a source of employment and income. It provides jobs through activities such as crop farming, animal farming, poultry farming, fish farming, agricultural processing, and marketing.
They also learned that farmers earn income by selling crops, animals, fish, eggs, milk, and other agricultural products. Agriculture also creates employment opportunities for people involved in processing, transportation, and marketing.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Many products people use every day are made from materials obtained from farms. For example, cotton is used to make clothes, cocoa is used to make chocolate, rubber is used to make tyres, and timber is used to make furniture.
These basic materials obtained from agriculture are called raw materials. Industries use them to manufacture different goods for people.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about agriculture as a source of raw materials for industries and the importance of agricultural raw materials to industries.
MEANING OF RAW MATERIALS
Raw materials are natural or basic materials used to produce or manufacture other goods.
Many industries depend on agriculture for the raw materials they need to make different products.
AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF RAW MATERIALS
Agriculture provides raw materials from crops, animals, forests, and other agricultural activities.
Examples include:
Agricultural Produce - Raw Material Used For - Industrial Products
- Cotton - Textile industries - Clothes and fabrics
- Cocoa - Food industries - Chocolate and cocoa products
- Rubber - Rubber industries - Tyres, gloves, and other rubber products
- Palm oil - Soap and food industries - Soap, cooking oil, and cosmetics
- Cassava - Food industries - Flour, starch, and other products
- Sugarcane - Food industries - Sugar
- Timber - Wood and paper industries - Furniture, paper, and other wood products
- Hides and skins - Leather industries - Shoes, bags, and belts
- Milk - Dairy industries - Yoghurt, cheese, and other dairy products
- Groundnut - Food industries - Groundnut oil and other products
IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURAL RAW MATERIALS TO INDUSTRIES
Agriculture provides raw materials that:
1. Support industries: Industries depend on agricultural materials to produce goods.
2. Create employment: Industries provide jobs for people who process agricultural raw materials.
3. Generate income: Farmers earn money by selling agricultural products to industries.
4. Promote local production: Local raw materials encourage the production of goods within the country.
5. Reduce dependence on imported materials: Industries can use locally available materials.
6. Support economic development: Agricultural and industrial activities contribute to the growth of the economy.
7. Encourage farming: The demand for raw materials encourages farmers to produce more.
EXAMPLES OF INDUSTRIES THAT USE AGRICULTURAL RAW MATERIALS
- Textile industry: Uses cotton to make clothes and fabrics.
- Food industry: Uses cocoa, cassava, milk, groundnut, and other farm products.
- Rubber industry: Uses natural rubber to make tyres and other products.
- Leather industry: Uses hides and skins to make shoes, bags, and belts.
- Furniture industry: Uses timber to make furniture.
- Soap and cosmetics industry: Uses palm oil and other agricultural products.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Agriculture is an important source of raw materials for industries.
- Products such as cotton, cocoa, rubber, palm oil, timber, hides, skins, milk, and groundnut are used to manufacture many useful goods.
- Therefore, agriculture and industries depend on each other for growth and development.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People use clothes and medicines in their everyday lives. Some of the materials used to produce these items come from agriculture.
For example, cotton is used to make clothes, wool is used to make warm clothing, and leather is used to make shoes and bags. Some plants and animal products are also used in the production of certain medicines and health products.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about agriculture as a source of materials for clothing and medicine production and the importance of these materials.
LESSON 1 - AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF MATERIALS FOR CLOTHING
Agriculture provides materials used to make clothes and other clothing items. These materials are obtained from plants and animals.
Examples include:
- Cotton: Used to make clothes, shirts, trousers, and other fabrics.
- Wool: Obtained from sheep and used to make warm clothing.
- Silk: Obtained from silkworms and used to make fabrics.
- Leather: Obtained from animal hides and skins and used to make shoes, belts, bags, and other items.
IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURAL MATERIALS FOR CLOTHING
Agricultural materials:
1. Provide materials for making clothes.
2. Provide materials for making shoes, bags, and belts.
3. Create employment in textile and leather industries.
4. Provide income for farmers.
5. Support local industries.
6. Reduce dependence on imported materials.
LESSON 2 - AGRICULTURE AS A SOURCE OF MATERIALS FOR MEDICINE
Agriculture also provides plants and animal products that are used in the production of some medicines and health products.
Examples include:
- Aloe vera: Used in some skin and health products.
- Neem: Used in some traditional and pharmaceutical preparations.
- Ginger: Used in some preparations and health products.
- Garlic: Used in some traditional and health preparations.
- Honey: Used in some health products and preparations.
- Castor oil: Obtained from castor seeds and used in some pharmaceutical and personal-care products.
IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURAL MATERIALS FOR MEDICINE

1. Provide ingredients used in some medicines and health products.
2. Support pharmaceutical and health-related industries.
3. Provide income for farmers.
4. Create employment in farming and processing.
5. Encourage the cultivation of useful plants.
6. Support local production of health products.

6. Neem - Leaves/bark - Some health preparations
7. Ginger - Rhizome - Some health products
8. Honey bees - Honey - Some health products
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Agriculture provides important materials for clothing and medicine production.
- Crops, animals, and their products supply materials such as cotton, wool, silk, leather, honey, and plant extracts.
- These materials support industries, provide employment and income, and contribute to the well-being of people.

ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about agriculture as a source of food, employment, income, raw materials, clothing, and medicine. This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how agricultural products can be exported to other countries to earn foreign exchange.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Nigeria produces many agricultural products that are useful both within the country and in other countries. When products such as cocoa, cashew nuts, sesame seeds, ginger, rubber, and cotton are sold to other countries, Nigeria receives payment in foreign currencies.
The money earned through international trade is called foreign exchange. Agriculture therefore helps Nigeria earn foreign exchange while also providing income and employment.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about agriculture as a means of foreign exchange, agricultural products that can be exported, and the importance of agricultural exports to Nigeria.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE
Foreign exchange is the money or currency a country receives from other countries through international trade and other transactions.
When Nigeria sells agricultural products to other countries, it receives payment in foreign currencies such as US dollars, pounds sterling, or euros.
AGRICULTURE AS A MEANS OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE
Agriculture can help Nigeria earn foreign exchange through the exportation of agricultural products to other countries.
Examples of agricultural products that can be exported include:
- Cocoa: Used to make chocolate and other products.
- Sesame seeds: Used as food and for producing oil.
- Cashew nuts: Exported as food and used in food processing.
- Ginger: Used as food, spice, and in some health products.
- Rubber: Used to manufacture tyres and other rubber products.
- Cotton: Used to produce textiles and clothing.
- Palm products: Used for food, soap, cosmetics, and other products.
LESSON 2 - IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE IN EARNING FOREIGN EXCHANGE
Agriculture helps the country to:
1. Earn foreign currency: Exported agricultural products bring money from other countries.
2. Support economic development: Foreign exchange helps support economic activities.
3. Create employment: Farming, processing, packaging, transportation, and export activities provide jobs.
4. Provide income to farmers: Farmers earn money by selling agricultural products.
5. Promote exports: Agriculture increases the amount of Nigerian products sold abroad.
6. Support industries: Agricultural products provide raw materials for local industries.
7. Improve international trade: Agricultural exports help Nigeria participate in international trade.
LESSON 3 - HOW AGRICULTURE EARNS FOREIGN EXCHANGE
The process can be explained simply:
Farmers produce agricultural products
↓
Products are processed and packaged
↓
Products are exported
↓
Foreign buyers pay for them
↓
Nigeria receives foreign exchange.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Agriculture is an important means of earning foreign exchange for Nigeria.
- By producing and exporting products such as cocoa, cashew nuts, sesame seeds, ginger, rubber, cotton, and palm products, Nigeria can earn money from other countries while providing employment and income for its people.

SUMMARY
Pupils learned that foreign exchange is money or currency received from other countries through international trade. They learned that Nigeria can earn foreign exchange by exporting agricultural products such as cocoa, cashew nuts, sesame seeds, ginger, rubber, and cotton.
They also learned that agricultural exports provide income to farmers, create employment, support industries, promote international trade, and contribute to economic development.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Agriculture involves many different activities. Some people grow crops, while others rear animals, catch or rear fish, manage forests, or provide services to farmers.
These different areas of agricultural activities are known as branches of agriculture. People such as farmers, fishermen, veterinarians, foresters, agricultural extension workers, engineers, and marketers play important roles in agricultural production.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the branches of agriculture, the activities carried out under each branch, and the people involved in agricultural production.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF BRANCHES OF AGRICULTURE
Branches of agriculture are the different areas or fields of agricultural activities. Each branch focuses on a particular type of agricultural production.
MAJOR BRANCHES OF AGRICULTURE
1. Crop Production - This involves growing crops such as maize, rice, cassava, yam, beans, fruits, and vegetables.
2. Animal Husbandry - This involves rearing and caring for animals such as cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, and poultry.
3. Fisheries - This involves catching and rearing fish and other aquatic animals.
4. Forestry - This involves planting, managing, and conserving trees and forest resources.
5. Horticulture - This involves growing flowers, fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants.
6. Agricultural Engineering - This involves the use and maintenance of machines, tools, and equipment used in farming.
7. Agricultural Economics - This deals with the production, distribution, marketing, and use of agricultural products and resources.
LESSON 2 - PEOPLE INVOLVED IN AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION
Many people contribute to agricultural production. They perform different jobs that help food and other agricultural products reach consumers.
1. Farmers - They grow crops and rear animals for food and other purposes.
2. Fishermen and Fish Farmers - They catch fish or rear fish in ponds, tanks, and other suitable places.
3. Foresters - They manage, protect, and conserve forests and trees.
4. Agricultural Extension Workers - They teach farmers improved farming methods and provide useful agricultural information.
5. Veterinarians - They care for animals and help prevent and treat animal diseases.
6. Agricultural Engineers - They design, operate, and maintain farm machines and equipment.
7. Agricultural Marketers - They buy, sell, and distribute agricultural products.
8. Farm Labourers - They assist farmers with activities such as planting, weeding, harvesting, and caring for animals.
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF PEOPLE INVOLVED IN AGRICULTURE
People involved in agricultural production:
1. Produce food for people.
2. Provide raw materials for industries.
3. Create employment.
4. Generate income.
5. Help transport and market agricultural products.
6. Promote agricultural development.
7. Help improve food production through modern farming methods.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Agriculture has several branches, including crop production, animal husbandry, fisheries, forestry, horticulture, agricultural engineering, and agricultural economics.
- Different people, such as farmers, fishermen, foresters, veterinarians, extension workers, agricultural engineers, marketers, and farm labourers, work together to produce and distribute agricultural products.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Agriculture involves not only growing crops but also keeping and caring for animals. Farmers keep different animals such as cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits, chickens, ducks, and turkeys for various useful purposes.
The practice of keeping, feeding, caring for, and managing animals is known as rearing of animals. Domestic animals provide food, income, employment, raw materials, manure, transportation, and other benefits.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning of rearing animals, types of domestic animals, examples of domestic animals, and reasons for rearing domestic animals.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF REARING OF ANIMALS
Rearing of animals is the practice of keeping, feeding, caring for, and managing animals for useful purposes.
It involves providing animals with food, water, shelter, proper care, and protection from diseases.
Examples of animals that can be reared include cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits, chickens, ducks, and turkeys.
TYPES OF DOMESTIC ANIMALS
Domestic animals are animals that are kept and cared for by people for useful purposes.
1. Cattle - Cattle include cows and bulls. They are reared for meat, milk, hides and skins, and other purposes.
2. Goats - Goats are reared mainly for meat and milk. Their skins can also be useful.
3. Sheep - Sheep are reared for meat, milk, and wool.
4. Pigs - Pigs are reared mainly for meat.
5. Poultry - Poultry includes chickens, ducks, turkeys, and geese. They are reared for meat and eggs.
6. Rabbits - Rabbits are reared mainly for meat and their skins.
LESSON 2 - REASONS FOR REARING DOMESTIC ANIMALS
Farmers rear domestic animals for many reasons, including:
1. Food: Animals provide meat, milk, eggs, and other foods.
2. Income: Farmers earn money by selling animals and animal products.
3. Employment: Animal rearing provides jobs for farmers and other workers.
4. Raw Materials: Animal products such as hides, skins, wool, and feathers are used by industries.
5. Manure: Animal droppings can be used as organic manure to improve soil fertility.
6. Transportation: Some animals, such as cattle and donkeys, can be used for carrying loads.
7. Security: Some domestic animals, especially dogs, can help guard homes and farms.
8. Breeding: Farmers rear animals to produce young ones and increase their livestock.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Rearing of animals involves keeping, feeding, caring for, and managing animals for useful purposes.
- Domestic animals such as cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, poultry, and rabbits provide food, income, employment, raw materials, manure, transportation, and security.

- Healthcare: Protecting animals from diseases and treating sick animals.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils define rearing of animals and mention ways of caring for animals.
Step 3: Types of Domestic Animals
The teacher explains the different types of domestic animals:
- Cattle: Cows and bulls kept mainly for milk, meat, and hides.
- Goats: Kept mainly for meat and milk.
- Sheep: Kept for meat, milk, and wool.
- Pigs: Kept mainly for meat.
- Poultry: Chickens, ducks, turkeys, and geese kept mainly for meat and eggs.
- Rabbits: Kept mainly for meat and skins.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the domestic animals and state the products obtained from them.
Step 4: Reasons for Rearing Domestic Animals
The teacher explains that domestic animals are reared to:
- Provide food such as meat, milk, and eggs.
- Provide income to farmers.
- Create employment.
- Provide raw materials such as hides, skins, and wool.
- Provide manure for improving soil fertility.
- Provide transportation and carrying of loads in some cases.
- Provide security, especially through the use of dogs.
- Provide animals for breeding and increased livestock production.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the reasons for rearing domestic animals.
Step 5: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of rearing of animals.
- Group 2: Mention six types of domestic animals.
- Group 3: Match domestic animals with the products obtained from them.
- Group 4: State five reasons for rearing domestic animals.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 6: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning of rearing animals, types of domestic animals, products obtained from them, and reasons for rearing domestic animals.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 7: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of the meaning, types, and reasons for rearing domestic animals.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

CROP PRODUCTION: MEANING, TYPES AND IMPORTANCE OF CROP PRODUCTION
AGRICULTURE
PRIMARY 4 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 9
THEME - PREVOCATIONAL STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Branches of Agriculture and People Involved in Agricultural Production | Primary 4 (Basic 4) First Term Week 8 Agriculture
TOPIC - CROP PRODUCTION
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Crop Production
3. Importance of Crop Production
4. Examples of Crop Production Activities
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of crop production.
2. Mention four types of crop production.
3. Give examples of crops produced under different types of crop production.
4. State five importance of crop production.
5. Mention some activities involved in crop production.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the branches of agriculture and people involved in agricultural production. This lesson builds on that knowledge by focusing on crop production, its types, activities, and importance.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures of different crops
2. Samples of maize, beans, rice, cassava, and yam
3. Pictures of crop farms
4. Charts showing types of crop production
5. Samples of farm tools
6. Flashcards
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Crop production is an important part of agriculture. Farmers grow different crops such as maize, rice, cassava, yam, beans, fruits, and vegetables for food and other purposes.
Crop production involves growing and caring for crops from planting until they are ready for harvesting. Farmers carry out activities such as land preparation, planting, weeding, applying manure or fertiliser, controlling pests and diseases, and harvesting.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning of crop production, types of crop production, examples of crops, and the importance of crop production.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF CROP PRODUCTION
Crop production is the process of growing and caring for crops from planting until they are ready for harvesting.
It involves activities such as land preparation, planting, weeding, applying manure or fertiliser, controlling pests and diseases, and harvesting.
Examples of crops include maize, rice, cassava, yam, beans, tomatoes, pepper, and vegetables.
TYPES OF CROP PRODUCTION
1. Subsistence Crop Production - This is growing crops mainly to provide food for the farmer and the farmer’s family.
2. Commercial Crop Production - This involves growing crops mainly for sale and profit.
3. Mixed Crop Production - This involves growing two or more types of crops on the same farm.
4. Plantation Farming - This involves growing crops such as cocoa, rubber, oil palm, and tea on large farms.
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF CROP PRODUCTION
Crop production is important because it:
1. Provides food: Crops provide food such as maize, rice, yam, cassava, and vegetables.
2. Provides income: Farmers earn money by selling their crops.
3. Provides employment: Crop production creates jobs for farmers, farm labourers, marketers, and transporters.
4. Provides raw materials: Crops such as cotton, cocoa, and rubber provide materials for industries.
5. Provides foreign exchange: Exporting crops to other countries can help Nigeria earn foreign exchange.
6. Supports industries: Agricultural products are used in processing and manufacturing industries.
7. Provides animal feed: Some crops and crop residues are used to feed livestock.
LESSON 3 - EXAMPLES OF CROP PRODUCTION ACTIVITIES
1. Clearing and preparing the land
2. Planting seeds or seedlings
3. Weeding
4. Applying manure or fertiliser
5. Controlling pests and diseases
6. Watering or irrigating crops
7. Harvesting crops
8. Storing harvested crops
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Crop production is an important branch of agriculture that involves growing and caring for crops until harvest.
- It provides food, income, employment, raw materials, and foreign exchange, and supports the development of industries.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Crop production is the process of _______.
A. rearing only animals
B. growing and caring for crops
C. growing and caring for crops
D. making farm tools
2. Which of the following is an example of crop production?
A. Growing maize
B. Rearing goats
C. Catching fish
D. Keeping bees
3. Growing crops mainly to provide food for the farmer and family is called _______.
A. commercial crop production
B. plantation farming
C. subsistence crop production
D. mixed farming
4. Growing crops mainly for sale and profit is called _______.
A. subsistence crop production
B. commercial crop production
C. backyard farming
D. home gardening
5. Which of the following is an importance of crop production?
A. It causes food shortage
B. It destroys industries
C. It prevents employment
D. It provides food
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. The process of growing and caring for crops is called _______.
7. Growing crops mainly for the farmer’s family is called _______ crop production.
8. Growing crops mainly for sale and profit is called _______ crop production.
9. _______ is an example of a crop produced by farmers.
10. Crop production provides _______ for people to eat.
C. True or False
11. Crop production involves growing and caring for crops. _______
12. Maize and cassava are examples of crops. _______
13. Commercial crop production is mainly for sale and profit. _______
14. Subsistence crop production is mainly for export to other countries. _______
15. Crop production can provide employment and income. _______
D. Matching
16. Mixed Crop Production - A. Growing crops mainly for sale
17. Plantation Farming - B. Growing two or more crops on the same farm
18. Commercial Crop Production - C. Growing and caring for crops
19. Subsistence Crop Production - D. Growing crops mainly for family food
20. Crop Production - E. Growing crops on large farms
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. A 3. C 4. B 5. D
6. Crop production
7. Subsistence
8. Commercial
9. Maize
10. Food
11. True
12. True
13. True
14. False
15. True
16. Mixed Crop Production - B. Growing two or more crops on the same farm
17. Plantation Farming - E. Growing crops on large farms
18. Commercial Crop Production - A. Growing crops mainly for sale
19. Subsistence Crop Production - D. Growing crops mainly for family food
20. Crop Production - C. Growing and caring for crops
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that crop production is the process of growing and caring for crops from planting until harvesting.
They learned about subsistence crop production, commercial crop production, mixed crop production, and plantation farming.
They also learned that crop production provides food, income, employment, raw materials, animal feed, and foreign exchange.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What crops do farmers grow?
- Can you mention some crops you have seen on a farm?
- Why do farmers grow crops?
- What activities do farmers carry out before harvesting crops?
The teacher explains that growing and caring for crops is an important agricultural activity called crop production.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention crops they know.
Step 2: Meaning of Crop Production
The teacher explains that crop production is the process of growing and caring for crops from planting until they are ready for harvesting.
The teacher explains that activities involved in crop production include:
- Land Preparation: Preparing the land for planting.
- Planting: Putting seeds or seedlings into the soil.
- Weeding: Removing unwanted plants from the farm.
- Applying Manure or Fertiliser: Providing nutrients needed for healthy crop growth.
- Pest and Disease Control: Protecting crops from harmful pests and diseases.
- Harvesting: Gathering mature crops from the farm.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils define crop production and mention activities involved in crop production.
Step 3: Types of Crop Production
The teacher explains the different types of crop production:
- Subsistence Crop Production: Growing crops mainly to provide food for the farmer and the farmer’s family.
- Commercial Crop Production: Growing crops mainly for sale and profit.
- Mixed Crop Production: Growing two or more types of crops on the same farm.
- Plantation Farming: Growing crops on large farms, usually on a large scale.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the types of crop production and explain their meanings.
Step 4: Importance of Crop Production
The teacher explains that crop production:
- Provides food for people.
- Provides income for farmers.
- Creates employment.
- Provides raw materials for industries.
- Provides animal feed.
- Provides foreign exchange through exportation.
- Supports economic development.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the importance of crop production.
Step 5: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of crop production.
- Group 2: Mention four types of crop production.
- Group 3: Mention five activities involved in crop production.
- Group 4: State five importance of crop production.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 6: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning of crop production, its types, activities involved in crop production, and its importance.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 7: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of the meaning, types, and importance of crop production.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
